passages.title: Sunday Trip
sentences: On Sunday, Sam went to the train museum with Grandma Rose.
They saw a big black steam train.
Sam climbed into the driver's seat.
Then they rode a small train around the park.
Sam bought a postcard of the steam train.
He put it on his wall at home.

passages.title: Leo's Spelling Test
sentences: Leo had a spelling test on Friday.
He studied the words every night.
On Friday, he spelled every word right.
After the test, Ben asked, "Was it hard?"
Leo grinned and said, "It was a piece of cake!"
Ben laughed and said, "You studied a lot!"

passages.title: The Young Crab and His Mother
sentences: A young crab lived on a sandy beach with his mother.
One morning, they walked across the wet sand together.
Like all crabs, the young crab walked sideways.
"You should walk straight ahead," said his mother.
"Walking sideways is the wrong way."
"I will try," said the young crab. "Please show me how."
His mother lifted her claws and began to walk.
But her legs went sideways too, just like his.
She tried again and again, but she could not walk straight.
At last, she stopped and laughed.
"Now I understand," she said. "I should not tell you to do something that I cannot do myself."

credit.title: The Young Crab and His Mother
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Art Show
sentences: On Friday night, Maya's comic was in the school art show.
She had to talk about it in front of the parents.
Before her turn, Ben gave her a thumbs-up.
"Break a leg!" he said with a smile.
Maya laughed and walked to the front of the room.
She talked about her comic, and everyone clapped.
Ana stayed home that night.
She had a cold and felt under the weather.
After the show, Maya sent her a photo of the comic.

passages.title: The Fox and the Grapes
sentences: One hot afternoon, a hungry fox walked slowly along an old stone wall.
Above the wall, a bunch of ripe purple grapes hung from a twisting vine.
The grapes looked sweet and full of juice, and the fox wanted them very much.
He stepped back, ran forward and jumped as high as he possibly could.
His nose was still far below the lowest grapes.
He tried again and again, but every jump was too short.
At last, the fox sat down on the warm ground, tired and thirsty.
He looked up at the grapes one more time, and then he turned and walked away.
"Those grapes are probably sour anyway," he said. "I did not want them."

credit.title: The Fox and the Grapes
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Priya's Big Day
sentences: The Harbor Town robot contest was on Saturday at the library.
All week, Priya worked on her rover after school.
On Thursday, she also had a science quiz.
"I need to hit the books tonight," she told her mom.
She read her science notes at the kitchen table until bedtime.
On Saturday, Priya's rover drove through the maze in fifty seconds.
The judges gave her the blue ribbon for first place.
Sam, Maya and Leo cheered from the front row.
On the walk home, Priya held the ribbon and smiled the whole way.
"I'm on cloud nine," she said to Sam.
Sam laughed and said, "I can tell!"

passages.title: The Lion and the Mouse
sentences: A big lion was sleeping in the warm sun.
A small mouse ran across his paw and woke him up.
The lion grabbed the mouse with his huge paw.
"Please let me go," said the mouse. "One day I will help you."
The lion smiled at the idea of such a tiny helper, but he let the mouse go.
A few days later, the lion stepped into a rope net in the tall grass.
He pulled and pulled, but the ropes held him tight.
The mouse heard the lion roar and ran to him.
She chewed through the ropes with her sharp teeth.
Soon the lion was free.
The lion thanked the mouse, and they became good friends.

credit.title: The Lion and the Mouse
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
sentences: A shepherd boy had a job watching the sheep on a hill near a village.
The days were long and quiet, and he felt bored.
One morning, he shouted, "Wolf! A wolf is chasing the sheep!"
The people in the village ran up the hill to help.
They saw only sheep eating grass, and the boy laughed.
The next day, he played the same trick again.
Then one evening, a real wolf came out of the woods.
The boy shouted "Wolf!" as loudly as he could.
This time, the people thought it was another trick, so they stayed home.
The wolf chased the sheep far away into the hills.

credit.title: The Shepherd Boy and the Wolf
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The North Wind and the Sun
sentences: One day, the North Wind and the Sun argued about which of them was stronger.
Just then, they saw a traveler walking down a road in a warm coat.
"Let us see who can make him take off his coat," said the Sun.
The North Wind went first.
He blew a cold, hard wind at the traveler.
But the harder he blew, the tighter the traveler held his coat around him.
At last, the North Wind stopped trying.
Then the Sun came out from behind a cloud.
She shone gently and warmly on the traveler.
Soon the traveler felt hot, so he opened his coat.
Then he took it off and sat down in the shade of a tree.

credit.title: The North Wind and the Sun
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Three Days at the Skate Park
sentences: Leo wanted to learn a new trick at the skate park.
The trick is called an ollie.
In an ollie, you jump, and the board jumps with you.
On Monday, Leo tried it and fell off.
On Tuesday, he tried ten more times.
Sam sat on a bench and ate an apple.
On Wednesday, Leo and his board jumped up together.
He did his first ollie!

credit.title: Three Days at the Skate Park
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: A Table Outside the Library
sentences: The Harbor Middle School soccer team needed new balls.
Ana and Ben had a plan to get the money.
They would hold a bake sale on Saturday.
On Friday, they baked oat cookies with Grandma Rose.
Ben made a big sign with green letters.
On Saturday, they set up a table outside the library.
The wind blew their sign over twice.
By noon, they had sold every cookie.
They made forty dollars, enough to buy four new balls.
At practice on Wednesday, the whole team cheered.

passages.title: The Octopus
sentences: An octopus has many clever ways to stay safe.
It can change the color of its skin in less than a second.
Then its skin can match the rocks and sand around it.
If a hungry fish swims close, the octopus can squirt dark ink.
The ink makes a cloud in the water.
The octopus hides behind the cloud and swims away.
An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze into tiny cracks to hide.
An octopus also has eight arms and three hearts.

passages.title: Freight Trains
sentences: A freight train carries goods instead of people.
It uses different kinds of cars to carry different kinds of loads.
A boxcar is a big metal box with a sliding door on each side.
It keeps things like paper and canned food dry.
A tank car is shaped like a long tube.
It carries liquids, such as oil or corn syrup.
A hopper car has doors on the bottom.
When the doors open, coal or grain pours out.
A flatcar has no walls and no roof, so it can carry logs, steel beams or big shipping boxes.
The engine that pulls all these cars is called a locomotive.
Some freight trains are more than a mile long.

passages.title: Hailstones
sentences: Hailstones are balls of ice that fall from big thunderstorm clouds.
Each hailstone grows inside the cloud, one layer at a time.
It starts as a tiny piece of ice high up in the cloud, where the air is very cold.
Strong winds inside the storm push it up and keep it from falling.
Drops of icy cold water hit the ice and freeze onto it.
Each time this happens, the hailstone gets a little bigger.
At last, it gets too heavy for the wind to hold up, and it falls to the ground.
If you cut a hailstone in half, you can often see its layers as rings.
Most hailstones are about the size of a pea.
The biggest one ever found in the United States fell in South Dakota in 2010.
It was about as wide as a volleyball.

passages.title: History Week
sentences: The Harbor Town library asked students to make displays for Town History Week.
Sam decided to build a model of the old train line that once ran along the harbor.
First, he found an old map in the library's history room.
The map showed where the tracks and the station used to be.
Then he and Grandma Rose built the tracks on a big wooden board.
Grandma Rose brought muffins from her bakery for lunch.
Sam made tiny trees from bits of green sponge.
Pixel watched from under the table and wagged his tail.
On the first day of the display, Sam's small electric train ran all the way around the board.
Many visitors stopped to watch it.
An old man said he had ridden that train when he was a boy.

passages.title: Robots on Mars
sentences: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, and it has two small moons.
It looks red because its dusty ground contains a lot of rust.
Mars is so far away that no person has ever traveled there.
Instead, scientists send rovers, which are robot cars built to drive on another planet.
Rovers explore Mars for us, and they send what they find back to Earth.
Driving a rover is not like driving a toy car with a remote.
A radio message takes from about 3 to 22 minutes to get from Earth to Mars.
Because of this delay, the team on Earth cannot steer the rover while it drives.
Instead, they send it a plan for the day, and the rover uses its cameras to steer around rocks on its own.
Each rover carries science tools, such as cameras, a drill and a laser.
The rover named Curiosity zaps rocks with its laser to find out what they are made of.
Curiosity also found signs that a lake once filled the crater where it landed.
Another rover, Perseverance, drills into rocks and seals small samples inside metal tubes.
Scientists hope to bring those tubes back to Earth one day.
Perseverance did not travel alone.
It carried a small helicopter named Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet in 2021.

passages.title: Minerals
sentences: A mineral is a solid that forms naturally in the ground.
Minerals are not made by plants or animals.
Some minerals are very hard, like diamond, and some are soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, like talc.
Many people think minerals belong only in rock collections and museums.
In fact, minerals dug from the earth are inside many things you use at home every day.
Start in the kitchen.
Table salt is a mineral called halite.
Some salt is dug from mines deep underground, and some is made by drying out seawater.
The glass in your windows and cups is made mostly from sand that is rich in quartz.
Next, look around your room.
The gray part inside a pencil is graphite mixed with clay.
Many people call it lead, but pencils do not contain any lead.
The walls of many homes are made of boards filled with gypsum, a soft white mineral.
The wires that carry electricity are often made of copper, a metal that comes from rocks dug out of mines.

words.means: on its own in the earth, not made by people

passages.title: Up the Ramp
sentences: Every Wednesday after school, the robotics club met in Ms. Ortiz's science room.
This month, Priya's team had one goal: build a rover that could climb a steep wooden ramp.
Ms. Ortiz had built the ramp to copy a rocky hill on Mars.
The room still smelled of fresh paint, because the walls had just been painted blue.
On the first try, the rover's smooth plastic wheels spun in place, and it slid back down.
Priya studied the wheels and decided they needed more grip.
Leo glued thin strips of rubber around each wheel.
On the second try, the wheels gripped the wood, but the rover tipped over backward halfway up.
Ms. Ortiz asked the team where the heaviest part of the rover was.
It was the battery, which sat high on top of the rover.
The team moved the battery down low, between the front wheels.
On the third try, the rover moved slowly up the ramp and stopped at the very top.
Everyone clapped, and Leo cheered so loudly that a teacher from next door looked in.
Priya wrote each change in her notebook so the team would remember what had worked.

passages.title: Dinosaur Fossils
sentences: When people think of dinosaurs, they often picture giant skeletons standing in museum halls.
The word dinosaur means "terrible lizard," and the large dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.
Most dinosaur bones never became fossils, because a bone turns to stone only after a long series of steps.
The first step had to happen quickly.
Soon after a dinosaur died, its body needed to be buried by mud or sand, often at the bottom of a river or lake.
This covering protected the bones from wind, rain and hungry animals.
The soft parts of the body broke down, but the hard bones and teeth remained.
Over thousands of years, more layers of mud and sand piled on top.
Their weight slowly pressed the lower layers into solid rock.
Meanwhile, water seeped through the ground, carrying tiny bits of minerals.
The minerals filled the small spaces inside the bones and hardened there.
Slowly, the bones turned into stone that kept their original shape.
Millions of years later, movements of the earth can push those rock layers up toward the surface.
Wind and rain wear away the rock until part of a fossil is exposed.
Scientists who study fossils, called paleontologists, dig them out carefully with small picks and brushes.
Some fossils are not bones at all, such as footprints and eggs.

passages.title: Coral Reefs
sentences: Many people who see a coral reef for the first time think it is made of colorful rocks or plants.
In fact, a coral reef is built by animals.
Tiny animals called coral polyps build reefs over thousands of years, and those reefs become homes for a huge number of sea creatures.
Most coral polyps are smaller than a pencil eraser.
Each one has a soft body shaped like a tube, with a ring of tentacles around its mouth.
A polyp takes minerals from seawater and uses them to build a hard cup of limestone around its body.
When a polyp dies, its hard cup stays behind, and new polyps grow on top of it.
Over thousands of years, millions of these cups pile up into a reef.
Reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor.
Even so, about one quarter of all the kinds of animals in the ocean spend part of their lives on reefs.
Small fish hide in the cracks, crabs and shrimp live among the branches, and sea turtles visit to feed.
Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which protect them from bigger fish.
Tiny living things called algae live inside many corals and help give them their bright colors.
The largest reef system in the world is the Great Barrier Reef, off the coast of Australia.
It stretches for about 2,300 kilometers, which is more than 1,400 miles.

passages.title: Fog in the Harbor
sentences: For two weeks, Ms. Ortiz's science class had been preparing for a field trip to Gull Island to study the animals in its tide pools.
Sam had read the ferry timetable so many times that he could recite every departure time.
On the morning of the trip, however, a thick fog came in from the sea and covered the whole harbor.
At the dock, a sign said that the ferry would not run until the fog cleared.
Several students groaned, and Sam felt disappointed, because he had wanted to ride the ferry.
Ms. Ortiz did not cancel the lesson, though.
She explained that tide pools also formed on the rocky shore below the lighthouse, only a short walk away.
The class zipped up their rain jackets and followed her along the harbor path, past the Lighthouse Café, which smelled of cinnamon rolls.
The tide was low, so many small pools of seawater were left between the rocks.
The students found purple sea stars, tiny crabs and green sea anemones holding on to the rocks.
Maya sketched each animal in her notebook, while Priya counted how many of each kind they saw.
Sam drew a map of the shore and marked the spot where every pool was.
Back at school, the class combined their sketches, counts and map into a large poster about the animals of the harbor shore.
Ms. Ortiz hung it in the hallway and promised that they would still visit Gull Island next month.

passages.title: How Bees Make Honey
sentences: Honeybees make honey from nectar.
Nectar is a sweet juice inside flowers.
A bee drinks the nectar with its long tongue.
It keeps the nectar in a special stomach just for carrying it.
Then the bee flies back to its hive.
There, it passes the nectar to other bees.
They put the nectar into small wax cells.
The bees fan the cells with their wings to dry out some of the water.
The nectar gets thick and sticky, and it turns into honey.
The bees close each cell with a wax lid.
In winter, when there are no flowers, the bees eat the honey.
A honeybee has five eyes.
Its wings beat more than 200 times every second.

passages.title: How a Compass Works
sentences: Hikers, sailors and pilots often carry the same simple tool.
A compass uses a tiny magnet to show which way is north, and that helps people find every other direction.
Inside a compass is a thin needle that is a magnet.
The needle sits on a pin, so it can spin freely.
Earth itself acts like a giant magnet.
Because of this, the needle always turns until one end points north.
On most compasses, that end is painted red.
Once you know where north is, you can find the other directions.
If you face north, south is behind you, east is on your right, and west is on your left.
Hikers lay a map flat and turn it until north on the map points the same way as the needle.
Keep a compass away from magnets and big metal things, because they can pull the needle the wrong way.
People in China used compasses more than 900 years ago.
Sailors used them to steer their ships when clouds hid the stars.

passages.title: The Ferry Game
sentences: Ana and Ben decided to make their own board game for Game Day at the library.
In their game, each player steers a ferry from island to island and picks up passengers.
Maya drew the islands and the ferries on a big piece of blue cardboard.
Ben wrote twelve rules on two whole pages.
On Wednesday, the twins tested the game with Sam and Leo.
Sam and Leo kept asking questions about the rules, and one game took almost two hours.
Leo yawned and said he had forgotten whose turn it was.
That night, the twins sat at the kitchen table and cut the rules from twelve to five.
Ben ate a whole bowl of popcorn while they worked.
On Friday, they tested the game again, and it took only thirty minutes.
This time, Sam and Leo laughed and asked to play again.
On Game Day, people waited in line to try the ferry game.

passages.title: How a Video Game Is Made
sentences: When you play a video game, you see only the finished game.
A team of people made it, and they may have worked on it for months or even years.
Making a video game takes many steps, and each step needs people with different skills.
It starts with designers, who decide what the player's goal is and what rules the game will follow.
They sketch the levels on paper and often build a quick, rough version called a prototype.
Playing the prototype shows them early whether the idea is fun.
Next, artists draw the characters, the buildings and the worlds.
Animators make those characters walk, jump and wave.
Programmers write code, which is a long list of exact instructions for the computer.
For example, the code might say that when the player presses a button, the character jumps.
Meanwhile, sound designers record footsteps and splashes, and composers write the music.
Before the game is released, testers play it again and again to find bugs, which are mistakes in the code.
A bug might let a character walk through a wall or fall through the floor.
The team fixes each bug and tests the game again.
Large games can take hundreds of people several years to make, but some small games are made by just one person.

credit.title: How a Video Game Is Made
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: How Instruments Make Sound
sentences: A guitar, a trumpet and a drum look very different, and they sound different too.
Yet every instrument makes sound in the same way: it makes something vibrate.
A vibration is a very fast movement back and forth.
It pushes on the air around it, and the moving air carries the sound to your ears.
Each family of instruments makes its vibrations in a different way.
In string instruments, such as the guitar and the violin, the strings vibrate.
A guitar player plucks the strings, and a violin player pulls a bow across them.
Short, tight or thin strings vibrate faster and make higher notes.
The hollow wooden body of the instrument makes the sound louder.
In wind instruments, the air inside a tube vibrates.
A flute player blows across a hole near one end, and a trumpet player buzzes both lips against the mouthpiece.
A longer tube makes a lower note, which is one reason a tuba sounds much deeper than a trumpet.
In percussion instruments, such as drums, the player hits something to make it vibrate.
When a drummer strikes a drum, its tight skin, called the drumhead, shakes up and down.
A large drum makes a low boom, and a small drum makes a higher tap.

passages.title: How Glaciers Shape the Land
sentences: A glacier is a huge, thick mass of ice that moves slowly across the land.
Glaciers may look as if they are standing still, but over thousands of years they carve valleys, carry giant boulders and change the shape of the land.
Today, glaciers cover about one tenth of all the land on Earth, mostly in the cold regions near the poles and high in the mountains.
A glacier forms in a place where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer.
Year after year, new layers of snow pile up on top of the old ones.
The weight of the upper layers presses the snow below into solid ice.
When the ice becomes thick and heavy enough, it begins to flow slowly downhill under its own weight.
Most glaciers move so slowly that a person watching one would not notice it moving.
As a glacier moves, it freezes onto loose rocks and drags them along underneath it.
These rocks scrape and grind the ground below, wearing away soil and even solid rock.
A river usually cuts a narrow valley shaped like the letter V.
A glacier carves a much wider valley with steep sides and a flat bottom, shaped like the letter U.
Glaciers can also carry boulders as big as houses for hundreds of kilometers.
When the climate warms and a glacier shrinks, it leaves behind clues about where it once was.
Long ridges of rock and sand, called moraines, mark the places where the ice stopped.
Boulders that do not match the rock around them show how far the ice carried them.
Scientists study these clues to learn how far the ice spread long ago.
Glaciers also store about two thirds of all the fresh water on Earth.

passages.title: Two Hundred Muffins
sentences: On Thursday afternoon, the Harbor Town soccer league ordered two hundred blueberry muffins from Rose's Bakery for its end-of-season party.
The muffins had to be ready by ten o'clock on Saturday morning.
Grandma Rose had baked large orders before, but on Friday evening her big electric mixer made a loud grinding noise and stopped.
The repair shop could not fix it until Monday, and mixing that much batter by hand would take one person all night.
Sam stopped by the bakery with Pixel, saw the problem and sent a message to his friends.
By seven o'clock, Ana, Ben and Leo had arrived, washed their hands and tied on aprons.
Grandma Rose gave each person one job.
Ana measured the flour and sugar, Ben and Leo stirred the batter in four big bowls, and Sam filled the muffin trays.
Grandma Rose watched the ovens and set a timer for every batch.
Leo had a white streak of flour across his nose for an hour before anyone told him.
Because each person stayed at one job, nobody had to stop and switch tasks, and the work went faster than anyone expected.
By ten o'clock that night, every muffin was baked, cooled and packed into boxes.
On Saturday morning, Mr. Okafor lent them a bike trailer, and Sam and Leo pulled the boxes to the soccer field.
They arrived at 9:45, fifteen minutes early.
The players cheered when they saw the muffins, and the coach thanked Grandma Rose and her helpers.
Pixel stayed close to the boxes the whole time, sniffing the air.

passages.title: The Plow Train
sentences: Last winter, a big storm dropped deep snow on Harbor Town.
The snow covered the train tracks.
A special train with a plow on the front came to help.
The plow pushed the snow off the tracks.
Its bright lights helped the driver see in the storm.
By morning, the trains could run again.
Sam watched the plow train from his window with Pixel.

passages.title: Maya's Rock Box
sentences: It was raining, so Maya stayed inside.
She got out her box of rocks and minerals.
She wanted to know which rocks were hard.
She tried to scratch each one with a nail.
The nail made a line on the soft talc.
It did not scratch the quartz at all.
Maya put the hard rocks in one pile.
Then she drew a chart of her rocks.

passages.title: The Moon
sentences: The Moon is covered with round holes called craters.
Long ago, many rocks from space hit the Moon.
Each rock made a crater when it hit.
The Moon has no wind and no rain.
So the craters do not wear away.
The Moon goes around Earth about once a month.
Twelve people have walked on the Moon.

passages.title: Emperor Penguins
sentences: Emperor penguins live in Antarctica, where it is very cold.
They have many ways to stay warm.
Under their skin is a thick layer of fat.
Their short feathers are packed close together.
The feathers keep out the wind and the icy water.
On the coldest days, the penguins stand close in a big group.
This group is called a huddle.
They take turns in the warm middle.
Emperor penguins are the tallest of all penguins.
They dive deep under the ice to catch fish.

passages.title: Saturday's Game
sentences: On Saturday, Ana and Ben had a big soccer game.
But that morning, heavy rain fell on Harbor Town.
The soccer field was covered with deep puddles.
Coach Novak sent a message to the team.
The game would be played in the school gym instead.
At first, Ben was disappointed, because he liked the big field.
Ana's socks got wet on the walk to the gym.
In the gym, the ball bounced fast on the wooden floor.
The team passed quickly and won by two goals.
After the game, Ben said the gym was more fun than he expected.

passages.title: Rainbows
sentences: You can see a rainbow when the sun shines through rain.
Sunlight looks white, but it is made of many colors.
When sunlight goes into a raindrop, the drop bends the light.
Each color bends by its own amount, so the colors spread out.
The light comes back out of the drop as a band of colors.
Red is always on the outside.
Violet is on the inside.
To see a rainbow, stand with the sun at your back.
Sometimes a second, fainter rainbow shows up above the first one.
Its colors are in the opposite order.

passages.title: Finding the Rooms
sentences: A new student joined Sam's class on Monday.
She did not know where any of the rooms were.
At lunch, Sam drew her a map of Harbor Middle School.
He drew the office, the gym and the library.
He marked their classroom with a red star.
He also drew a small train in one corner, just for fun.
The next morning, the new student used the map to find the music room by herself.
She smiled and thanked Sam.

passages.title: Popcorn
sentences: Popcorn is a special kind of corn.
It pops because of a tiny drop of water inside each kernel.
Each kernel has a hard shell with starch inside.
When the kernel gets hot, the water turns into steam.
The steam pushes harder and harder on the shell.
At last, the shell bursts open with a pop.
The hot starch puffs out and becomes white and fluffy.
People have eaten popcorn for thousands of years.
Some people like it with butter, and some like it with salt.

passages.title: Sea Turtles
sentences: A sea turtle spends almost its whole life in the ocean.
But when a female is ready to lay eggs, she makes a long trip.
She swims back to the same beach where she hatched many years before.
Some sea turtles swim thousands of kilometers to get there.
Scientists think they use Earth's magnetic field to find their way.
At night, the mother turtle crawls up onto the sand.
She digs a hole with her back flippers and lays about one hundred eggs.
Then she covers the eggs with sand and swims back to sea.
About two months later, the baby turtles hatch and hurry to the water.
Sea turtles cannot pull their heads into their shells the way many land turtles can.
The biggest kind, the leatherback, can weigh more than 500 kilograms.

passages.title: The High Note
sentences: Ms. Gray chose Ana to play a short trumpet solo at the winter concert.
The solo had one very high note near the end.
At first, that note squeaked every time Ana tried it.
Ms. Gray showed her how to take a deep breath before the hard part.
Every day after school, Ana played the solo ten times in her bedroom.
In the next room, Ben wore headphones while he played a video game.
After two weeks, the high note sounded clear almost every time.
On the night of the concert, the school gym was full of families.
Ana stood up, took a deep breath and played her solo.
The high note rang out clear and strong.
Afterward, her parents gave her a bunch of yellow flowers.

passages.title: Triceratops
sentences: Triceratops was a plant-eating dinosaur with a huge head.
Its name means "three-horned face."
Scientists think each part of that head helped it in a different way.
Two long horns grew above its eyes, and a short horn grew on its nose.
It may have used its horns to protect itself from hungry Tyrannosaurus.
A wide plate of bone, called a frill, grew from the back of its skull.
The frill may have helped Triceratops show off to others of its kind.
At the front of its mouth was a sharp beak, like a parrot's beak.
It used the beak to bite off tough plants.
Triceratops lived in what is now North America.
It lived about 66 million years ago, near the end of the time of the dinosaurs.

passages.title: Saturday's Goalkeeper
sentences: On Thursday, Coach Novak had a problem.
The team's goalkeeper had a bad cold and could not play in Saturday's game.
Coach Novak asked Ben to play in goal instead.
Ben had never been the goalkeeper before, and he felt nervous.
On Friday, Ana kicked ball after ball at him during practice.
She told him to keep his eyes on the ball until it reached his hands.
By the end of practice, Ben's shirt was covered in grass stains.
The game started at ten o'clock on Saturday morning.
Ben stopped six shots, and the team won the game 2 to 1.
Afterward, Coach Novak asked Ben to be the backup goalkeeper for the rest of the season.
Ben's grass-stained shirt took two washes to come clean.

passages.title: How Trains Roll
sentences: A train is very heavy and moves fast, but it almost never slides off the track.
The reason is the special shape of its wheels.
Train wheels are made of steel, and they roll on steel rails.
Each wheel has a lip, called a flange, on its inside edge.
The flanges sit just inside the two rails.
If the train starts to slide sideways, a flange bumps the rail and holds the train in place.
The wheels are also slightly cone-shaped, so each one is wider near the flange.
On a curve, the outer wheel rolls on its wider part, and the inner wheel rolls on its narrower part.
That helps the train turn smoothly.
Steel wheels on steel rails roll very easily, so trains use less fuel than trucks to carry the same load.
Many early trains in the 1800s were pulled by steam engines.

passages.title: Robot Vacuums
sentences: A robot vacuum cleans the floor while nobody pushes it.
To do this, it uses sensors to learn about the room around it.
A sensor is a part that notices something, such as a touch or a change in light.
When the robot bumps into a chair, a bump sensor in the front tells it to turn.
Cliff sensors underneath point down at the floor.
If the floor drops away, like at the top of the stairs, the robot backs up.
Some robots also use a camera or a laser to make a map of the home.
With a map, the robot can clean in neat rows instead of wandering around.
When its battery runs low, it finds its way back to its charger.
Most robot vacuums are thin enough to clean under a bed.
Some families even give their robot vacuum a name.

words.means: a thin, strong beam of light
the base it plugs into to get power

passages.title: The Ranger's Helpers
sentences: After a windy week, many branches had fallen across the trail in Story Woods.
The park ranger asked for helpers to clear the trail on Saturday.
Sam, Leo and Maya signed up, and each of them got a pair of thick gloves.
First, they dragged the branches off the path and piled them under the trees.
The ranger said the piles would become homes for mice and beetles.
Next, they filled muddy holes in the trail with gravel.
Leo found a beetle with a shiny green back and named it Gus.
Last, Maya painted new yellow marks on the trees so hikers would not get lost.
At noon, they ate lunch on a log by the creek.
By three o'clock, the whole trail was clear again.
The ranger thanked them and gave each of them a Story Woods patch.

passages.title: Searching for Gold
sentences: Long ago, many people searched for gold in streams with a simple metal pan.
This is called panning, and it works because gold is much heavier than sand and pebbles.
First, a person scoops sand and gravel from the bottom of a stream into the pan.
Then they hold the pan under the water and shake it from side to side.
The heavy gold sinks to the bottom of the pan.
Next, they tip the pan and swirl it, so the water washes the light sand over the edge.
After many swirls, only a little dark sand is left.
If they are lucky, tiny flakes of gold shine in it.
Gold is about nineteen times heavier than the same amount of water.
In 1848, gold was found in California, and thousands of people rushed there to pan for it.
Today, some people still pan for gold for fun.

words.means: to move it around in a circle

passages.title: The Game Shelf
sentences: The Harbor Town library has a shelf of board games that anyone can borrow.
But many games kept coming back with pieces missing.
One chess set had lost two pawns, and a word game was missing half its letter tiles.
Ana and Ben offered to help Mrs. Hall fix the problem.
First, they counted the pieces in every box.
Then they wrote a checklist and taped it inside each lid.
The checklist said exactly how many pieces belonged in the box.
Ana also found small bags for the cards and dice.
Mrs. Hall put up a sign that asked players to count the pieces before they returned a game.
The game shelf is next to a big window, where the sun shines in the afternoon.
A month later, almost every game came back with all its pieces.
To celebrate, Ben beat Ana at chess for the first time.

passages.title: The Space Station
sentences: About 400 kilometers above Earth, a small crew lives and works inside the International Space Station.
The station circles the planet about every 90 minutes, so the crew sees around 16 sunrises each day.
Because everything on board floats, even simple daily tasks must be done in a new way.
Sleeping is a good example, because in space there is no real up or down.
Each crew member sleeps in a sleeping bag tied to the wall of a cabin about the size of a closet.
Drinks come in sealed pouches with straws, so the liquid cannot float away in drops.
Salt and pepper are mixed into liquids, because loose grains would drift into machines and eyes.
Floating may sound restful, but it is hard on the human body.
On Earth, gravity pulls on bones and muscles all day, and that work keeps them strong.
In space, without that pull, they slowly grow weaker.
So the crew must exercise for about two hours every day.
They run on a treadmill while straps hold them down, and they lift weights on a special machine.
People have lived on the station without a break since the year 2000.
Crew members from many countries have shared it.

passages.title: The Deep Ocean
sentences: Sunlight shines into the top part of the ocean, but it fades as the water gets deeper.
Below about 1,000 meters, the water is completely dark, and it stays very cold all year.
The weight of all the water above presses down hard on everything below.
In the darkness, many animals make their own light.
This light is called bioluminescence, and it comes from chemicals inside their bodies.
The anglerfish has a glowing lure that hangs in front of its mouth.
Small fish swim toward the light, and the anglerfish snaps them up.
Other animals flash light to confuse hunters or to find others of their kind.
Food is hard to find in the deep, because plants cannot grow without sunlight.
Much of the food is bits of dead plants and animals that drift down from above, called marine snow.
Many deep-sea fish move slowly to save energy, and some have huge mouths so they can eat almost anything they find.
Many deep-sea animals also have soft bodies with lots of water inside.
This helps them live under the heavy water without being crushed.
The deepest known spot in the ocean, called the Challenger Deep, is about 11,000 meters down.

passages.title: Priya Leads the Workshop
sentences: Every Saturday morning in February, the Harbor Town library held a robot workshop for younger children, and Mrs. Hall asked Priya to lead it.
Priya had built her own rover, so she thought teaching eight-year-olds to build simple robots would be easy.
She arrived early, set out boxes of motors, wheels and wires, and wrote all the steps on the whiteboard.
Within ten minutes, every table had a problem.
One boy had connected his wires backward, so his robot drove in reverse.
Two girls both wanted to hold the only screwdriver.
A small boy in a dinosaur shirt had not started at all, because he did not understand the first step.
Priya realized that her steps were clear to her, but not to someone who had never seen a motor before.
She asked everyone to stop, and she started again, one step at a time.
This time, she held up each part, said its name, and waited until every table was ready before she moved on.
She gave the two girls separate jobs, so one held the screwdriver while the other read the next step aloud.
By the end of the hour, six small robots were rolling across the carpet.
The boy in the dinosaur shirt asked if he could come back next week.
On the walk home, Priya told her mom that teaching was harder than building, but she wanted to do it again.

passages.title: Ready for Winter
sentences: In places where winters are cold, food becomes hard to find, and the days grow short and freezing.
Animals that live in these places cannot buy a coat or switch on a heater.
Instead, most of them get through the winter in one of three ways: they leave, they sleep, or they change how they live.
Some animals travel to warmer places for the winter, which is called migration.
Many geese fly south in long lines shaped like the letter V.
Monarch butterflies from eastern North America fly thousands of kilometers to forests in Mexico.
Other animals hibernate, which means they go into a deep sleep for the winter.
During hibernation, an animal's heart beats much more slowly, and its body cools down.
A woodchuck's heart may slow from about 80 beats a minute to fewer than ten.
It lives on fat that it stored by eating extra food in the fall.
Many animals stay active all winter but change their bodies or their habits.
Squirrels bury nuts in the fall and dig them up when snow covers the ground.
The snowshoe hare grows a white coat that matches the snow, and its wide back feet help it walk on top of the snow.
Some squirrels forget where they buried their nuts, and those nuts can grow into new trees.

passages.title: The Bike Route
sentences: Sam wanted to ride his bike to the lookout in Lantern Peaks with Leo and Priya on Saturday.
The shortest way was Ridge Road, but it was steep, narrow and busy with trucks.
So on Thursday evening, Sam spread a map of Harbor Town on the kitchen table to look for a better route.
He used a green pencil to trace every street that had a bike lane.
Then he studied the thin brown lines on the map, called contour lines, which show how steep the land is.
Where the lines are packed close together, the ground is steep, and on Ridge Road they almost touched.
Sam found another road, Mill Road, where the lines were spread far apart as it curved gently around the hill.
It was two kilometers longer, but it had a bike lane almost the whole way.
On Friday, Sam showed his route to Mr. Okafor at the bike shop.
Mr. Okafor agreed that it was a smart choice, and he pumped up the tires on all three bikes.
He also gave Leo a bell shaped like a fish, and Leo rang it the whole afternoon.
On Saturday, the three friends rode Mill Road to the lookout without having to walk their bikes once.
Priya said the longer road had felt easier than a shorter, steeper one.
At the top, they ate apples and looked down at the harbor.

words.means: the way you plan to go
going up sharply, so it is hard to climb
to draw over the line of

passages.title: Inside a Piano
sentences: A piano looks like a large wooden box with keys, but inside it is a machine with thousands of parts.
Every note you hear begins when you press a key and a small hammer strikes tight steel strings.
Each key works like a seesaw.
When you press down the front of the key, the back end rises and pushes a small wooden hammer upward.
The hammer is covered with soft felt, and it hits the strings and then quickly falls back.
The strings vibrate, and a large, thin wooden board called the soundboard makes the sound louder.
A piano has 88 keys and more than 200 strings.
Most notes use two or three strings tuned to exactly the same note, which makes them louder.
Long, thick strings make low notes, and short, thin strings make high notes.
Together, the strings pull on the frame so hard that the frame must be made of iron.
When you let go of a key, a felt pad called a damper drops onto the strings and stops the sound.
If you press the right pedal, all the dampers lift, so the notes keep ringing.
A piano tuner usually adjusts the strings once or twice a year so the notes stay correct.

passages.title: The Class Picnic
sentences: At the end of the school year, Ms. Ortiz's class planned a picnic at Harbor Park, and Ana and Maya offered to plan the food.
They wanted every student to be able to eat a full lunch.
That was harder than it sounded, because Ana cannot eat peanuts or tree nuts, and two classmates do not eat meat.
First, the girls made a list of every food they could think of.
Then they crossed out anything with nuts, such as the peanut butter cookies, the trail mix and the walnut bread.
Next, they made sure there was a choice without meat for each part of the meal.
Beside the turkey sandwiches, they added cheese and tomato sandwiches.
Maya drew a menu card for each dish, with a small picture and a list of what was in it.
On the sandwich card, she drew a tiny cartoon tomato wearing sunglasses.
Grandma Rose baked oat bars for dessert, using a recipe with no nuts at all.
On the day of the picnic, the sun was warm, and a breeze came off the harbor.
Students read the menu cards and filled their plates without needing to ask any questions.
Everyone ate a full lunch, and only crumbs were left of the oat bars.

passages.title: Dinosaur Sizes
sentences: Many people picture every dinosaur as a giant that shook the ground with each step.
Some dinosaurs really were huge, but others were no bigger than a chicken.
In fact, dinosaurs came in many sizes, from tiny to enormous.
The biggest dinosaurs were plant eaters with long necks and long tails, called sauropods.
One of them, Argentinosaurus, may have been more than 30 meters long.
That is longer than two school buses parked end to end.
Long necks let sauropods reach leaves that other animals could not.
At the other end, some meat-eating dinosaurs were small and quick.
Compsognathus was about the size of a turkey, and it hunted small lizards.
Microraptor was about the size of a crow.
It had feathers on both its arms and its legs.
The smallest dinosaurs alive today are smaller still.
Scientists agree that birds are a kind of dinosaur, so the tiny bee hummingbird is a dinosaur too.
It is only about five centimeters long.

passages.title: Wind
sentences: You cannot see the wind, but you can see it bend trees and push clouds across the sky.
Wind is simply air that is moving from one place to another.
Air moves because the Sun warms some places more than others.
When the Sun heats the ground, the ground warms the air just above it.
Warm air spreads out and becomes lighter, so it rises.
Cooler, heavier air then flows in to fill the space it left behind.
That flow of air is the wind.
You can feel this happen at a beach on a sunny day.
Land heats up faster than water, so by afternoon the air over the sand is warmer than the air over the sea.
The warm air over the land rises, and cool air from the sea moves in to take its place.
This cool wind from the water is called a sea breeze.
At night, the land cools faster than the water, so the wind often turns around and blows out to sea.
Scientists measure wind speed with a tool called an anemometer, which has small cups that spin in the wind.
The fastest wind gust ever measured by an anemometer was 408 kilometers per hour, on an island near Australia in 1996.

passages.title: The Library Birthday
sentences: For the library's birthday, Mrs. Hall hid five puzzle clues around the building, and the first team to solve them all would win a box of new board games.
Sam, Maya, Priya and Leo formed a team and called themselves the Fast Four.
The first clue was a drawing of a bookshelf.
Maya, who studies every line when she draws comics, noticed tiny numbers hidden on the spines of the books.
The numbers led the team to shelf 551, where the next clue was taped.
The second clue was a code made of numbers, and Priya, who programs her rover, solved it in two minutes.
The third clue was a map of the library with a path drawn in dotted lines.
Sam turned the map until it matched the room, and he led everyone straight to the history room.
The fourth clue was a riddle that asked what has keys but cannot open a door.
Leo laughed, because he had heard that joke before.
The answer was a piano, and the last clue was taped under the lid of the old piano in the reading room.
The last clue asked a question about the history of Harbor Town, and the four friends solved it together.
They finished first, ten minutes ahead of the next team.
Mrs. Hall handed them the box of games and a bag of apples.
Leo suggested that they become the Fast Five so that Pixel could join next time.

passages.title: Searching the Stars
sentences: For thousands of years, people wondered whether other stars had planets circling them, the way Earth circles the Sun.
The question was hard to answer, because a planet near a distant star is far too dim, and too close to its bright star, to be seen in most telescopes.
Since the 1990s, however, astronomers have found thousands of these distant planets, called exoplanets, by looking for small clues instead of the planets themselves.
The most common clue is a tiny dip in a star's light.
If a planet passes in front of its star, as seen from Earth, it blocks a small part of the starlight.
A telescope that measures the star's brightness records a dip that repeats every time the planet goes around.
The size of the dip tells astronomers how big the planet is, and the time between dips tells them how long its year lasts.
Another clue is a slight wobble.
As a planet circles a star, its gravity tugs the star back and forth by a tiny amount.
Astronomers cannot see the star move, but they can measure tiny changes in the color of its light as it wobbles toward us and away from us.
A heavier planet causes a bigger wobble.
Space telescopes have made the search much faster.
One space telescope, named Kepler, watched about 150,000 stars at the same time and found more than 2,600 planets.
Today, the number of known exoplanets is more than 5,000, and some of them are about the same size as Earth.

passages.title: From Rock to Wire
sentences: The copper wires inside the walls of a house carry electricity to every light and outlet.
That copper began as rock deep in the ground, and turning it into wire takes several big steps.
Each step removes more of the rock, until almost pure copper is left.
Most copper comes from enormous open-pit mines, which look like giant bowls with steps carved into their sides.
Workers break the rock loose, and trucks as tall as a two-story house carry it away.
This rock, called ore, usually contains less than one percent copper.
That means a whole truckload of ore holds only a small amount of copper.
At a mill, machines crush the ore into a powder as fine as flour.
The powder is mixed with water and special chemicals in large tanks.
Air is bubbled through the tanks, and the bits of copper mineral stick to the bubbles and float to the top as a froth.
The froth is skimmed off, while the leftover rock sinks to the bottom.
Next, the copper powder is heated in a furnace until it melts.
Then electricity is used to remove the last unwanted materials, making copper that is more than 99 percent pure.
Finally, the pure copper is pulled through smaller and smaller holes until it becomes thin wire.
Copper is also easy to recycle, because old copper can be melted down and used again.
People have used copper for thousands of years.

words.means: a layer of bubbles on top
a very hot oven for melting metal

passages.title: The Skate Park Ramps
sentences: For months, the concrete ramps at the Harbor Town skate park had been cracking, and one of the metal rails had come loose.
Leo skated there almost every day, so he noticed every new crack.
He complained about it to anyone who would listen, but complaining did not fix a single crack.
Then Mrs. Hall showed him a notice at the library: the town council held a meeting on the first Monday of every month, and anyone could speak for three minutes.
Leo decided that three minutes was enough time if he used it well.
With Sam's help, he took photos of every crack and measured the longest one, which was almost a meter long.
Sam drew a map of the park and marked each damaged spot with a red dot.
Priya stood at the gate for a week with a clipboard and counted about two hundred visitors.
Ana and Ben collected signatures from forty skaters, parents and neighbors who wanted the park repaired.
Leo practiced his speech in front of Sam and Pixel until he could say it without reading his notes.
He also took out a joke he had planned to tell and put in Priya's count of visitors instead.
On the first Monday of the month, Leo wore his only button-up shirt to the town hall.
At the microphone, he showed the photos and the map, and he handed the council the list of signatures.
He spoke calmly and finished ten seconds before his three minutes were over.
Two weeks later, the council voted to repair the ramps and the rail before summer.
When the repairs were finished, Leo was the first to skate down the smooth new ramp.
He told his friends that the photos and the map had shown the problem better than his complaints ever had.

passages.title: Autumn Leaves
sentences: In many forests, autumn turns green hillsides into patches of yellow, orange and red.
It may seem that trees add new colors to their leaves, but most of those colors were hidden inside the leaves all summer.
Leaves are green because they are full of a chemical called chlorophyll.
Chlorophyll captures sunlight, and the tree uses that energy to make sugar from water and air.
Leaves also contain yellow and orange chemicals, but in summer there is so much green chlorophyll that it covers them up.
In autumn, the days grow shorter and the nights grow cooler.
The tree begins to get ready for winter, and it stops making new chlorophyll.
As the green fades, the yellow and orange that were there all along finally show.
Red and purple are different, because many trees make those colors only in the fall, from sugar trapped in the leaves.
Sunny days and cool nights help make the reds brighter.
Finally, a thin layer of cells grows where each leaf joins its twig.
The layer slowly cuts the leaf off, and the leaf falls to the ground.
There, fallen leaves break down and add food to the soil.

passages.title: The Wheelhouse
sentences: Sam had ridden the Harbor Town ferry dozens of times, but he had never been inside the wheelhouse, the room at the top where the captain steers.
So when Captain Ruth Lane invited his class on a tour, he was the first in line.
She explained that steering a ferry is not like driving a car, because the water has no painted lines or road signs.
Instead, a captain uses several tools together to find a safe path.
First, she unrolled a large paper chart, which is a map of the water instead of the land.
Tiny numbers covered the blue areas, and each one showed how deep the water was at that spot.
Sam noticed that the numbers grew small near Gull Island, where rocks lay just under the surface.
The ferry, she said, must always stay where the numbers are large enough.
Out the window, she pointed to red and green floating markers called buoys.
They mark the edges of the safe channel, the way lines mark the edges of a road.
When the ferry comes into the harbor, it keeps the red buoys on its right side.
Finally, she showed them two screens.
One was a radar screen, which shows nearby boats and land even in the dark, and the other showed the ferry's exact position from satellites.
Priya asked whether the ferry had an autopilot button, and Captain Lane said it did, but she always kept her hands near the wheel.
On the ride home, Sam drew his own chart of the harbor in his notebook, with the depth numbers he remembered.
He marked the rocks near Gull Island with a careful row of X's.

passages.title: Robot Arms
sentences: In many factories, some of the busiest workers are robot arms.
A robot arm can repeat the same movement thousands of times a day without getting tired.
That is why factories use robot arms for jobs that must be done exactly the same way every time.
The first factory robot arm went to work in a car factory in 1961.
A robot arm is built a little like a human arm.
It has joints that bend and turn, like a shoulder, an elbow and a wrist.
Each joint has its own electric motor, and a computer controls all the motors together.
At the end of the arm is a tool, which can be a gripper, a welder, a paint sprayer or even a suction cup.
In car factories, robot arms weld metal parts together and spray paint onto car bodies.
In food factories, they pack cookies into boxes and stack the boxes for shipping.
Some robots are so precise that they can place parts smaller than a grain of rice onto a circuit board.
Robots do not do every job in a factory, however.
People design the robots, write their programs and fix them when they break.
Many large robot arms work inside fences, because they move quickly and with great force.
Newer robots, called cobots, are smaller and slower, so they can work right next to people.

passages.title: Recording Day
sentences: The Harbor Town radio station invited Ms. Gray's students to record one song for its Friday evening show.
Ms. Gray chose six students: Sam brought his guitar, Priya her cello, Maya her flute, Ana her trumpet, Ben his keyboard and Leo his drums.
They had three hours in the music room to make a recording they were proud of.
On the first try, the recording sounded messy, because every sound bounced off the hard walls and floor.
Ms. Gray explained that this was an echo, and that soft things soak up sound.
The students hung blankets on the walls and laid a rug under the drums.
The second recording was much clearer.
Now, however, they could hardly hear Maya's flute, because the drums and the trumpet were much louder.
Ms. Gray moved the flute closer to the microphone and asked Leo to use soft brushes instead of sticks.
Ana played a little more quietly and pointed her trumpet slightly away from the microphone.
On the third try, Ben's keyboard went silent in the middle of the song, because its power cord had come loose.
Everyone wanted to stop, but Ms. Gray said they had time for one more try.
Ben taped the cord to the floor, and the group played the song again from the beginning.
This time, every instrument could be heard, and no one missed a note.
On Friday evening, Sam listened to the show in Grandma Rose's kitchen while Pixel slept under the table.
When the song ended, the host said it was one of the best student recordings the station had ever played.

passages.title: Bats in the Dark
sentences: Most bats hunt at night, when it is too dark to see insects flying through the air.
Many bats find their food by using sound instead of sight, with a skill called echolocation.
Echolocation means finding things by listening to echoes.
As a bat flies, it makes short, high-pitched calls through its mouth or nose.
Most of these calls are too high for people to hear.
When a call hits an object, such as a moth or a tree branch, part of the sound bounces back as an echo.
The bat's large ears catch the echo.
From the echo, the bat can tell where an insect is, how big it is and which way it is moving.
An echo that comes back quickly means the object is close.
As a bat closes in on an insect, it calls faster and faster, sometimes up to about 200 times a second, so it can follow every turn.
Using echolocation, a single little brown bat can catch hundreds of insects in one night.
This makes bats helpful to farmers, because many of the insects they eat damage crops.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly.
Not all bats use echolocation, however, and many large fruit bats find their food by sight and smell.

passages.title: The Fossil Lab
sentences: Maya had visited the dinosaur hall at the Harbor Town museum many times.
But she had never seen the room behind the glass wall, where fossils are cleaned.
That changed when Dr. Bell invited the rock club to spend a Saturday in the fossil lab.
On a long table sat a lump of rock wrapped in a hard white jacket of plaster.
Dr. Bell explained that her team had found a dinosaur leg bone in that rock and had wrapped it in plaster to protect it on the trip to the museum.
She handed Maya a tool that looked like a tiny, buzzing pen.
It was called an air scribe, and it chipped away rock a few grains at a time.
Dr. Bell showed her how to hold it at a low angle and stop as soon as the color changed, because the fossil bone was darker than the rock around it.
After an hour of careful work, Maya had uncovered a patch of bone no bigger than a postage stamp.
Mr. Varga, who was working at the next table, said that preparing one large bone can take months.
Maya was surprised, but she understood why when she brushed away the dust and saw tiny lines in the bone.
Rushing could break those lines, and they might show scientists how the dinosaur's bones had grown.
At lunch, the club ate sandwiches on the museum steps and watched pigeons hop around.
In the afternoon, Maya uncovered a second patch of bone, and Dr. Bell wrote Maya's name in the lab notebook next to that day's work.
Before she left, Maya drew the bone in her sketchbook, with every tiny line in place.
She asked Dr. Bell if she could come back next month to keep working on it.

words.means: a white paste that dries very hard
cleaning a fossil out of its rock

passages.title: From Dough to Bread
sentences: A ball of bread dough can double in size while it sits in a warm kitchen, even though nobody touches it.
The work is done by yeast, a living organism so small that billions of them fit in a teaspoon.
Bread rises because yeast makes gas, and the dough traps that gas in millions of tiny bubbles.
Yeast is a kind of fungus, like a mushroom, but each one is a single cell.
When yeast is mixed into dough with water, it becomes active and begins to feed on sugars in the flour.
As it feeds, it gives off a gas called carbon dioxide, the same gas you breathe out.
Wheat flour contains proteins that form a stretchy net called gluten when the dough is mixed and kneaded.
Kneading, which means pressing and folding the dough, makes the gluten net stronger.
The net stretches around each bubble of gas like a tiny balloon, so the gas cannot escape.
As more gas is made, the bubbles grow, and the whole dough puffs up.
In the hot oven, the gas bubbles expand even more, and the bread rises one last time.
The heat kills the yeast and sets the gluten net, so the bread keeps its shape.
When you look at a slice of bread, the small holes you see are where the gas bubbles used to be.
Some flat breads, such as tortillas, are usually made without yeast, so they stay thin.
People have baked bread with yeast for thousands of years.

passages.title: Down the Big Hill
sentences: Leo pushed off at the top of the hill.
His skateboard was a rocket.
The trees went by in a green blur.
At the bottom, he stopped and laughed.
Then Sam rode down very slowly.
"You are a snail today," Leo said with a grin.
Sam grinned back and said, "A careful snail."

passages.title: The Last One in the Library
sentences: Maya was the last one in the library.
The room was a quiet cave.
Only one lamp was still on.
Then the bell rang for closing time.
Maya packed six thick books into her bag.
Her bag was a rock on her back as she walked home.
At home, she unpacked the books one by one.

credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: Ana's First Note
sentences: Ana played her trumpet in the band show.
Her first note was a bright sunrise.
Everyone in the room sat up and listened.
Ben clapped the loudest of all.
After the show, Ana said her legs were jelly.
She sat down until they felt strong again.
Later, Ben told her that the band sounded great.

passages.title: Pixel in the Snow
sentences: Snow fell all night on Harbor Town.
In the morning, the yard was a white blanket.
Pixel ran out and rolled in the snow.
His black fur was soon covered in white dots.
Sam laughed and called him a little snowman.
Then they went inside to get warm.
Pixel shook the last snow off his fur by the warm fire.

passages.title: The Science Fair Table
sentences: On the morning of the science fair, the gym was busy.
Every table was covered with posters, wires and small machines.
Priya set up her rover next to a tall model volcano.
Her stomach was a washing machine, spinning and spinning.
When the first judge came to her table, Priya took a deep breath.
She showed how the rover's camera sent pictures to her tablet.
The judge watched closely and wrote some notes.
Then he smiled and said, "This rover is a little explorer."
After he left, Priya felt calm again.
Her stomach was still at last.

passages.title: The Storm Over the Harbor
sentences: Dark clouds rolled over the harbor in the afternoon.
The wind was a wild horse, running through the streets.
Grandma Rose closed the bakery shutters.
Sam helped her carry the chairs inside.
Then heavy rain came down on the roof.
Thunder boomed over the water, and Pixel hid under the table.
Sam sat beside him and spoke in a soft voice.
By evening, the storm had passed.
The harbor was a mirror, smooth and still.
The next morning, Sam and Grandma Rose carried the chairs back outside.

passages.title: Three Tests in One Week
sentences: Ben had three tests in one week.
On Monday night, his homework was a mountain on his desk.
He did not know where to start.
His mom helped him make a list.
They put the math test first, because it came first.
Ben did one small part of the list each night.
By Thursday, the mountain was a small hill.
On Friday, he finished the last test and walked home.
He smiled the whole way.
His mom said the list was a good plan for next time too.

passages.title: Saturday at the Bakery
sentences: Every Saturday morning, Grandma Rose's kitchen was a beehive.
Bakers hurried from the ovens to the tables and back again.
Sam's job was to fold the boxes.
He folded them so fast that Grandma Rose called him a machine.
At noon, the last tray of muffins came out of the oven.
The smell was a warm hug that filled the whole street.
People walking past stopped and came inside.
By one o'clock, every muffin was sold.
Sam folded the empty boxes flat for next week.

passages.title: The Night Train Home
sentences: On the last night of the school trip, Ms. Ortiz's class rode the night train from Pine Bay back to Harbor Town.
Outside the window, the dark fields were an ocean, and the farmhouse lights were small boats far away.
Sam pressed his forehead to the cold glass and tried to count them.
Inside, the train car was a warm, humming cocoon.
Most of the class had fallen asleep with their jackets over their knees.
Maya drew the moon in her sketchbook, and Priya read a book about Mars with a small flashlight.
Near midnight, the train slowed down beside the harbor.
The conductor walked through the car and said, "Harbor Town, next stop."
Sam looked at the map on the wall, where a red line showed every station they had passed.
The line was a long thread that had pulled them all the way home.

passages.title: The Rover That Would Not Turn
sentences: For two weeks, Priya's rover had a problem she could not solve.
Every time she told it to turn left, it spun in a slow circle instead.
The problem was a locked door, and she could not find the key.
She checked the wheels, the battery and every wire.
She read her code line by line, three times.
Nothing was wrong that she could see.
At robotics club, Mrs. Hall looked over her shoulder and pointed at one number in the code.
"Your turn speed is ninety, not nine," she said.
Priya changed one number, and the rover turned left in a neat, quick curve.
The fix was a tiny key that opened the whole door.
Priya laughed and wrote the number on a sticky note so she would never forget it.
