passages.title: Clean Beach Day
sentences: On the first Saturday in May, Harbor Town holds Clean Beach Day.
This year, Ms. Ortiz asked her science class to help.
Sam, Priya and Leo met the rest of the class at the harbor beach at ten o'clock.
Each student got gloves, a bag and a grabber stick.
Priya counted every bottle cap she picked up, and she found sixty-two.
Leo carried the full bags up to the big bin by the road.
Sam walked along the edge of the water and pulled out a long tangle of fishing line.
Ms. Ortiz said fishing line can trap gulls and seals, so it must go in the bin.
By noon, the class had filled eighteen bags.
The beach was clean, and the gulls had space to walk on the sand again.
Grandma Rose brought muffins for everyone who helped.

passages.title: The Repair Café
sentences: On the last Sunday of each month, the big room at the Harbor Town library turns into a Repair Café.
People bring things that are broken, and helpers show them how to fix them.
The idea is simple: if a thing can be fixed, it should not go in the trash.
This month, Mr. Okafor set up a bike stand by the windows.
By the end of the day, he had fixed eleven bikes that their owners had planned to throw away.
Most of them needed only new brake pads or a little oil on the chain.
At the next table, Priya helped a boy whose toy robot would not move.
She opened its case and found that one wire had come loose from the battery.
Ten minutes later, the robot rolled across the table.
Grandma Rose brought a tray of lemon bars for the helpers, and they were gone by noon.
Before the café closed, the librarian added up the day's work.
Forty-three things had been fixed, from lamps and toasters to a torn backpack.
All of them went home with their owners instead of into the trash.

passages.title: How Gulls Open Clams
sentences: On a windy afternoon, Sam sat on the hill above the tide pools on Gull Island.
He had come to watch the ferry, but he watched the gulls instead.
One gull picked up a clam from the wet sand at the edge of the water.
It flew high over the rocks and opened its beak.
The clam fell and hit the rocks with a sharp crack.
The gull flew down and ate the soft part inside the broken shell.
Soon, Sam saw three more gulls doing the same thing.
One gull dropped its clam on the soft sand, and the shell did not break.
That gull picked the clam up again and flew back over the rocks.
Sam wrote down each step in his notebook, from the sand to the rocks to the open shell.
Back home, he showed his notes to Ms. Ortiz.
She said the gulls were using the hard rocks to open their food.

passages.title: Helping the Seal Pups
sentences: Every spring, seal pups are born on the quiet beaches of Gull Island.
A pup stays on the sand for several weeks while its mother swims out to catch fish.
If people come too close, the mother may stay away, and the pup cannot drink her milk.
So each spring, Ranger Jo asks for helpers to keep visitors at a safe distance.
This year, Ana and Ben signed up to help for a whole Saturday.
They took the early ferry, and the ride across the bay took forty minutes.
Their first job was to put up a long rope fence fifty meters from the pups.
Next, they stood by the path and showed visitors where to watch the pups through the free binoculars.
At noon, they ate their sandwiches at a picnic table near the dock.
In the afternoon, Ranger Jo gave them a clipboard to count the pups.
Ben counted nine pups, and Ana counted nine too, so they knew the number was right.
On the way back to the ferry, the wind blew Ben's hat into a bush.
Before Ana and Ben left, Ranger Jo told them that every pup on the beach had stayed safe that day.

passages.title: Checking the Wind
sentences: Sam spent a morning with Captain Ada at Windy Cape.
Before she takes her boat out, Captain Ada always checks the wind, and she showed Sam how.
First, she pointed to an orange windsock on a tall pole.
The windsock was full and straight, which meant the wind was strong.
It pointed toward the land, so the wind was blowing in from the sea.
Next, she asked Sam to look at the waves.
Many waves had white tops, and that is another sign of a strong wind.
Last, she turned on her weather radio and listened to the wind report for the coast.
The report said the wind would get even stronger after lunch.
So Captain Ada decided to keep her boat at the dock that day.
Sam wrote the three wind checks in his notebook so he could use them at home.

passages.title: The Best Place for Kites
sentences: Leo had flown kites in Harbor Town for years, but he had never flown one at Windy Cape.
Everyone in his kite club said it was the best place on the coast for kites.
On a Sunday in April, Leo finally went to find out why.
The first reason was easy to feel as soon as he stepped onto the cliff top.
A strong, steady wind blew in from the sea, and on most days it blows from the same side.
Nothing on the wide, grassy cliff top blocks the wind, because there are no trees or tall buildings.
The second reason was harder to see.
When the sea wind hits the cliffs, it is pushed upward, and it lifts kites high into the sky.
Leo let out his string, and his kite rose faster than it ever had in town.
Near the path, a small shop sold kites, string and key rings shaped like gulls.
Leo bought a cup of hot chocolate there and drank it on a bench.
By the end of the day, he agreed with his club: Windy Cape was the best place he had ever flown a kite.

passages.title: The Windsock
sentences: At the end of the runway at Cloud Hill, there is a tall pole with an orange and white tube of cloth on top.
Nell asked Mr. Lund what the tube was for.
"That is a windsock," he said. "It shows pilots what the wind is doing."
He explained that the wind blows into the wide end of the windsock.
The narrow end then points the same way the wind is going.
When the wind is strong, the windsock sticks straight out.
When the air is calm, it hangs down along the pole.
Pilots look at the windsock before they take off or land.
They like to take off into the wind, because it helps the plane lift into the air sooner.
Nell looked up at the windsock again.
It was hanging down, so today was a calm day for flying.

passages.title: Every Part Has a Job
sentences: On a clear afternoon, Captain Ada walked with Nell down the whole length of the runway at Cloud Hill.
It took them almost ten minutes, because the runway is long, flat and straight.
"A plane needs a lot of room to speed up before it can lift off," Captain Ada said.
"It also needs room to slow down after it lands."
At the far end, Nell stood next to a huge white number painted on the ground.
It was the number 27.
Captain Ada explained that runway numbers come from a compass.
A compass circle has 360 degrees, and west is at 270 degrees.
If you take away the last zero from 270, you get 27, so a plane that takes off from this end flies toward the west.
The other end of the same runway has the number 9, because a plane that takes off from there flies east, at 90 degrees.
On the way back, they passed small lights along both edges of the runway.
At night, these lights show pilots exactly where the runway is.
Captain Ada also picked up a loose stone and tossed it into the grass.
"Even a small stone can damage a spinning propeller," she said, "so we keep the runway clear."
Nell looked back at the long gray strip and saw that every part of it had a job.

passages.title: Dials in the Cockpit
sentences: Before the long flight, Captain Ada showed Nell the inside of the Kookaburra's cockpit.
In front of the pilot's seat was a panel full of round dials.
"Each dial tells me something I need to know," Captain Ada said.
First she pointed to the altimeter, which shows how high the plane is flying.
Next to it was the airspeed dial, which shows how fast the plane is moving through the air.
The compass shows which way the plane is heading, such as north or east.
Then she tapped the fuel gauge, which shows how much fuel is left in the tank.
"Over the sea, there are no roads or signs to follow," she said.
"These dials help me fly safely all the way to Australia."

passages.title: Over the Sea
sentences: Flying over the sea is very different from flying over land.
Over land, a pilot can look down and see roads, rivers and towns that match her map.
Over the sea, there is only water in every direction, and the waves all look alike.
There is also nowhere to land until the next island.
So before Captain Ada left Cloud Hill, she planned the flight with great care.
She marked two small islands on her map where she could stop for fuel.
She worked out how much fuel each part of the trip would need.
Then she added extra fuel, in case strong wind slowed the plane down.
She also packed a life jacket and a spare radio.
Out over the water, Captain Ada flew by her compass and her clock.
If the plane kept the right heading for the right number of minutes, she knew it would reach the next island.
Every hour, she called a radio station on the coast to tell them where she was.
Once, she saw a group of dolphins jumping far below, and she smiled.
But she kept watching her dials, because over the sea, careful planning is what keeps a pilot safe.

passages.title: Made for the Trees
sentences: Captain Ada watched a koala named Jarrah climb slowly up a tall gum tree.
"How does he hold on so well?" she asked Ranger Tess.
Ranger Tess explained that a koala's body is made for life in the trees.
Koalas have two thumbs on each front paw.
The thumbs help them hold on tight to branches.
Koalas also have long, sharp claws that grip the bark.
The pads on their paws are rough, so they do not slip.
When a koala sleeps, it sits in the fork of a tree, where two branches meet, so it does not fall.
Jarrah reached the top, wrapped his arms around a branch and closed his eyes.

passages.title: Why Banjo Sleeps
sentences: On her second day in Australia, Captain Ada went back to Bluegum Koala Sanctuary to see a koala named Banjo.
Banjo was asleep in the fork of his tree, just as he had been the day before.
"Does Banjo ever wake up?" Captain Ada asked with a laugh.
Ranger Tess smiled, because visitors ask her that question every day.
She explained that koalas sleep for 18 to 22 hours a day.
Their food is the reason.
Eucalyptus leaves are tough and full of strong oils, and they give a koala very little energy.
A koala's stomach needs a long time to break the leaves down.
So koalas rest for most of the day and night, and they save their energy for eating and climbing.
Ranger Tess also told Captain Ada that koalas are most awake in the evening and at night.
If she came back after six o'clock, she might see Banjo eat.
That evening, Captain Ada returned to the boardwalk with Ranger Tess.
Banjo was awake, pulling a branch toward him and chewing one leaf after another.

passages.title: Tools at the Weather Station
sentences: Next to the white dome at Star Point, there is a small weather station.
On Monday morning, Dr. Amal showed Maya how it works.
First, she opened a white wooden box with slanted slats on its sides.
Inside the box was a thermometer, which measures how warm the air is.
The slats let air flow through but keep the sun off the thermometer.
Next, she showed Maya a tall metal can that catches rain.
Each morning, Dr. Amal measures how much rain fell into it.
On top of the tallest pole, three small cups spun in the wind.
They measure how fast the wind is blowing.
Maya drew each tool and wrote its job next to it.
Dr. Amal uses all these numbers to tell when the sky will be clear for the telescope.

passages.title: Catching the Space Station
sentences: Sam and Grandma Rose spent two spring nights at Star Point.
On the first evening, Dr. Amal gave Sam a printed list of times for that week.
"These are the times when you can see the space station from here," she said.
Sam was surprised, because he had always believed the station was too small to see without a telescope.
Dr. Amal explained that the space station is about as long as a soccer field.
Its wide solar panels reflect sunlight, so it shines like a bright star.
Unlike a plane, it has no blinking lights, and it moves across the sky in a few minutes.
The best times to see it are soon after sunset or just before sunrise.
Then the sky is dark where you stand, but the station, high above, is still in sunlight.
At 8:42 that evening, Sam and Grandma Rose stood by the lamp path and looked west.
Grandma Rose brought a flask of warm tea and two wool blankets.
Right on time, a steady white light rose above the sea and moved across the sky.
Four minutes later, it faded away in the east.
Sam wrote the time in his notebook so he could tell Priya at school.

passages.title: The Key on the Big Map
sentences: The map room at Rail Coast station has one huge map on the wall.
It shows every island, from Home Island to Cloud Hill.
On Thursday, Mr. Haddad showed Sam how to read it.
First, he pointed to a box in the corner called the key.
The key shows each symbol on the map and tells what it means.
A black line with short cross lines is a railway.
A dashed blue line is a ferry route, and a small red square is a station.
Under the key, a scale bar shows that one centimeter on the map is two kilometers on the ground.
Sam used the key to find Shell Halt and Pier Station.
Then he used the scale bar to measure the Coast Line.
It was about twelve kilometers long.
While Sam worked, the big clock in the hall ticked loudly.

passages.title: Why Trains Need Signals
sentences: Ben rode the Coast Line from Pier Station with his mom on a windy afternoon.
Halfway to Rail Coast, the train stopped at a red signal and waited for three minutes.
Ben looked out of the window, but he could not see another train anywhere.
At Rail Coast, he asked Mr. Haddad why the train had to wait on an empty track.
Mr. Haddad said that trains cannot stop quickly like cars.
Their steel wheels roll on smooth steel rails, so they have very little grip.
A heavy train going fast can need hundreds of meters to stop.
A driver also cannot steer around anything on the track.
So the driver must know about danger long before the train gets close to it.
To keep trains apart, the line is split into sections called blocks.
Only one train may be in a block at a time.
A signal stands at the start of each block.
It shows red when a train is still in the block ahead.
A yellow light warns the driver that the next signal is red, so the train slows down.
Green means the line ahead is clear.
Ben's train had waited because a slow train was still in the next block, around a bend.
Ben now watches every signal from the window, and he has started a notebook of their colors.

passages.title: Rooms in a Shell
sentences: At the dig tent, Priya asked Dr. Bell what an ammonite was.
Dr. Bell said that ammonites were sea animals with soft bodies and hard, coiled shells.
They were related to the squid and the octopus of today.
Like a squid, an ammonite had arms near its head for catching food.
Its shell was split into many small rooms by thin walls.
The animal lived in the biggest room, at the open end of the shell.
The empty rooms held gas, which helped the ammonite float in the water.
As the ammonite grew, it built a new, bigger room and moved into it.
Most ammonites were small enough to hold in your hand, but a few grew wider than a bike wheel.
Ammonites lived in the sea for more than 300 million years.
They died out at the same time as the last dinosaurs.
Priya turned her own ammonite over and traced the curved lines where the walls had been.

passages.title: Stripes in the Cliff
sentences: On the last day of the dig, Ms. Ortiz brought her science class to Fossil Bay by boat.
Dr. Bell met them on the beach, below the tall gray cliff.
She asked the class to look closely at the cliff and say what they noticed.
Maya said that the cliff was made of thin stripes, some dark gray and some light gray.
Dr. Bell explained that each stripe is a layer of rock.
Each layer began as mud that settled on the floor of a sea, long ago.
New mud always settled on top of older mud, so the lowest layers are the oldest.
This means the layers can help scientists tell how old a fossil is.
A fossil found near the bottom of the cliff is older than a fossil found near the top.
Dr. Bell showed the class a chart of the cliff, with a drawing of a different ammonite beside each layer.
One kind, with a smooth shell, is found only in the lowest layers.
Another kind, with sharp ridges, is found only near the top.
So when a visitor finds a loose stone on the beach, the ammonite inside it shows which layer the stone fell from.
After the talk, the class ate lunch on the pier, and a gull tried to take Sam's sandwich.
Before the boat left, Dr. Bell gave each student a postcard with a drawing of the cliff.

passages.title: Under the Glass Floor
sentences: On the reef boat, Maya lay on the glass floor with her sketchbook.
Below her, an orange and white clownfish swam in and out of a sea anemone.
A sea anemone looks like a soft flower, but it is an animal.
Its long arms, called tentacles, can sting small fish that touch them.
Mari said the clownfish is safe, because a slimy coat on its skin stops the stings.
So the clownfish hides in the tentacles when a big fish comes near.
The clownfish helps the anemone too.
It chases away fish that try to eat the anemone's tentacles.
Mari said that the two animals help each other every day.
Maya drew the clownfish inside the anemone, with a big fish swimming away.
Then the boat moved on, and she closed her sketchbook.

passages.title: Inside the Ring of Coral
sentences: From the hill on Gull Island, Leo had seen a ring of white waves far to the west.
When he reached Reef Island, he learned what that white ring was.
It was the place where waves from the open sea meet the coral reef.
Mari explained that the reef is a ring of coral around the whole island, just under the surface of the sea.
Big waves roll in from the open sea, and when they reach the shallow reef, they break into white foam.
Most of their power is used up on the outer edge of the reef.
By the time the water reaches the lagoon, the waves are small and gentle.
Because the water is calm, sand sinks to the bottom, and the water stays clear.
Many young fish grow up in the calm lagoon, where they are safer than in the open sea.
Leo also noticed that Mari's boat was painted bright yellow, with a turtle on the side.
At lunch, he ate a mango and two cheese sandwiches on the beach.
In the afternoon, he swam in the lagoon, and there were almost no waves at all.
